recall.question: Budget 30 symbols; each frame has 4 payload and 2 checks. How much payload fits?
recall.why: Five whole six-symbol frames carry 20 payload symbols.

results.bookIdea: Redundancy trades transmission capacity for protection against communication errors.
results.boundary: Less redundancy carries {A}; more carries {B}. Every frame spends more of its fixed budget on extra bytes, leaving fewer payload bytes.
results.world: Does it hold up? This shows capacity cost only. It supplies no error channel, decoder or evidence that these extra bytes correct errors.

results.predictQuestion: How many full strings can five independent binary positions represent?

recall.question: Adding two binary positions multiplies the number of full strings by what?
recall.why: Each doubles the count, so the multiplier is 2×2=4.

results.bookIdea: Binary representation combines two possibilities per position.
results.boundary: Four bits permit {A}; five permit {B}. Each existing pattern receives two distinct extensions, so one extra position doubles the count.
results.world: Does it hold up? This exact count assumes two usable states per position. Carries, circuit speed and storage reliability are not modeled.

results.predictQuestion: Budget 30; batches use 10 work plus 5 switching. How much useful work completes?

recall.question: Budget 24: change work/setup 2/2 to 6/2. Which follows from this packing model?
recall.why: Useful work rises from 12 to 18; waiting and fairness are not represented.

results.bookIdea: Scheduling choices trade switching overhead against other performance goals.
results.boundary: Short batches complete {A}; long batches complete {B}. Fewer batches pay fewer switches, increasing useful work in this fixed budget.
results.world: Does it hold up? This accounts for setup only. Waiting time, fairness, concentration and the best real scheduling policy remain unmodeled.

results.predictQuestion: Errors are +4 or −4 equally often. What is mean signed error?

recall.question: Errors are +2 or −2 equally. Which follows?
recall.why: Signs cancel; absolute errors do not.

results.bookIdea: Measurement uncertainty requires more than a mean signed error.
results.boundary: Signed errors average {A}; magnitudes average {B}. Opposite signs cancel while each measurement remains four units from the target.
results.world: Does it hold up? This exact two-outcome calculation is not a measured uncertainty estimate or a confidence interval.

results.predictQuestion: Start at 100; 4 enter and 6 leave each step. What remains after five steps?

recall.question: A store starts at 20 and sends 3 to another store each step. After two steps, how much left it?
recall.why: Outward transfer totals 6; the remaining 14 answers a different question.

results.bookIdea: Energy accounting tracks transformations and transfers across a defined system boundary.
results.boundary: Balanced transfers retain {A}; extra outward transfer leaves {B}. The store’s decrease is accounted for by net transfer beyond its boundary.
results.world: Does it hold up? This conserves stated accounting units. It does not establish a physical law experimentally or represent every energy form.

results.predictQuestion: For 20 units at 80% and 80 at 20%, what is the combined rate?

recall.question: A report now includes only a high-rate subgroup. Does a higher average alone establish improvement?
recall.why: Changed inclusion can raise an aggregate with every subgroup rate unchanged.

results.bookIdea: Statistical conclusions depend on how data were selected and measured.
results.boundary: Both groups give {A}%; omitting group B gives {B}%. No unit’s stipulated rate improves; selection changes whose rates count.
results.world: Does it hold up? This exact aggregation shows selection sensitivity. It does not diagnose missingness in a real dataset.

results.predictQuestion: A binary design tree has a root and two outward rounds. How many nodes total?

recall.question: Three stages offer three independent choices each. How many complete designs?
recall.why: 3×3×3=27; total tree nodes additionally count prefixes.

results.bookIdea: Design involves searching alternatives under constraints on computation and attention.
results.boundary: One option per stage creates {A} nodes; two create {B}. Extra local choices multiply later alternatives in this collision-free tree.
results.world: Does it hold up? This counts enumerated candidates only. It does not measure quality, attention, partial-design reuse or search-heuristic performance.

results.predictQuestion: Starting at 1, what follows six tenfold multiplications?

recall.question: From 10³ to 10⁵ units, what factor separates the quantities?

results.bookIdea: Astronomical scales require reasoning across many orders of magnitude.
results.boundary: Six steps give {A}; seven give {B}. The additional step multiplies the accumulated scale by ten rather than adding ten.
results.world: Does it hold up? These are dimensionless scale factors, not dated cosmic events, an age estimate or the book’s calendar diagram.

results.predictQuestion: Starting at 8 angle units, what follows two halvings?

recall.question: Under the same rule, 12 angle units become what after two distance doublings?

results.bookIdea: Our view of Earth changes with the vantage point from which we see it.
results.boundary: One distance doubling gives {A}; two give {B}. The second halving acts on an already smaller angle rather than subtracting a fixed amount.
results.world: Does it hold up? This inverse-distance approximation assumes fixed object size and small angles. It is not an exact angular formula or spacecraft measurement.

results.predictQuestion: At 1.2 reading ticks per reference step, what accumulates in 10 steps?

recall.question: Clocks start at zero and advance 2 and 3 ticks per reference step. After four steps, what is their gap?
recall.why: Readings are 8 and 12; their gap is 4.

results.bookIdea: Elapsed time can differ between clocks in different physical conditions.
results.boundary: The prescribed rates give {A} and {B}. Matching initial readings do not prevent an accumulating gap when rates differ.
results.world: Does it hold up? This integrates prescribed readings only. No relativity equation, gravitational effect or clock measurement is supplied.

results.predictQuestion: An uncertainty starts at 0.01 and doubles five times. What is its final size?

recall.question: Uncertainty 0.1 triples three times. What is its final size?

results.bookIdea: Sensitivity to initial conditions can limit long-range prediction.
results.boundary: Doubling gives {A}; tripling gives {B}. Repeated amplification makes the multiplier increasingly important despite the same tiny starting uncertainty.
results.world: Does it hold up? This error recurrence is not a chaotic system. It proves neither chaos nor the accuracy of a weather forecast.

results.predictQuestion: Equal groups have expected rates 90% and 10%. What is their aggregate?

recall.question: Equal groups average 60% overall. Must each group be 60%?
recall.why: 80% and 40% also average 60%; the aggregate cannot identify both group rates.

results.bookIdea: Aggregate outcomes can conceal differences in how success is distributed.
results.boundary: Both mixtures give {A}% and {B}%. One separates high and low expected rates; the other gives both groups the aggregate rate.
results.world: Does it hold up? Rates are stipulated, not observed streaks. Equal averages establish neither equal randomness nor equal skill or individual outcomes.
